svg.aria-label: PMS color approval workflow: supply codes from the brand guideline, check layout only on the digital proof, approve a physical proof on the real substrate, then the approved sample governs the production run

g.text: From color choice to production standard
The proof-and-approval workflow that makes brand color repeatable across runs — four moves, each with its own job
Supply codes from the brand guideline
Pantone codes for each brand color,
ideally from an existing guideline.
No guideline? A physical sample or
high-resolution file, matched against
a Pantone fan deck — slower, and
committed to that matcher's deck.
Digital proof — layout only
Useful for checking layout and text,
but “not reliable for judging actual
color accuracy” — screens display
color differently from print.
Approving color from a digital proof
alone is the most common mistake.
Physical proof on the real substrate
Printed on the actual material — the
same paper, board or fabric as the
final product — with the specified
Pantone inks, shipped for approval.
Our version: the custom sample —
USD 25 + USD 20, made in 3–5 days.
The approved sample governs the run
It becomes the reference standard
for the full production run; any
deviation from it during mass
production is treated as a quality
issue, not a preference.
Reorders repeat against the same
approved reference.
The supplier test: a good manufacturer provides Pantone-matched physical proofs “as a standard step before mass production, not an optional add-on.”
One code, three materials (box, pouch, band) = three closely-related but not identical landings — managed by approving each material's proof, not by demanding the impossible from a single swatch.
Lamination moves color too: matte desaturates slightly and can tint; gloss enhances saturation — name the production material and finish in the specification, then approve color on it.
